q: How do you turn someone looking around into someone making things?
form: A map with a hole in it
subject: The journey model
heads: What the product had for them
rows: “Can I try this for a something simple ...”
A tool somebody else made, ready to run
“Can I trust this to be consistent for...”
That tool's own page, with how often it has run
“How can this fit into my workflow for ...”
The same empty box, reached last
end: The map is hers, drawn before any screen. The page is that map with its two empty places filled.
close: We map the change of mind first, then give each stage its place in the product.

q: How do you build for the expert without shutting out the beginner?
form: One page, read from three distances
subject: A single tool's page, and how dense it is
rows: Its name, one sentence, and Run
The long description, the steps it goes through, the tools most like it
Use spec, Get API, Get code
end: Nothing is hidden and nothing is taken out: “Giving description, detailed description, directly letting user see spec link etc. despite it being more information dense as a design solution”
close: We keep the depth, and build the way up to it.

q: How do you make the first visit worth a second?
form: Told backwards, from the last thing they see
subject: How a first visit ends
rows: A result. In the old product, that was all: “MIssing end point (what do i do with this now?)”
So the end was designed first
Under the result, the tools most like it. Beside it, a way to take it with you.
The run itself, one step at a time, so the wait reads as work.
A tool they did not have to make.
Which decides the first thing they see
“Let the user feel they have created / found / can show something of value for the time invested”
end: The story runs in reverse, and stops at the front page.
close: We design the first ten minutes to earn the next visit, not to close the sale.
imgs: The audit that found the missing end
Give them something they can use

q: How do you fix the onboarding when the onboarding isn't the problem?
form: The brief, with our notes in the margin
subject: What was asked for, line by line, against what the research said
rows: There was nothing to board. The only way in was an empty box.
Not simpler. Clearer about what it is for: “What are you really good at?”
The words were the team's, not the user's: “Create a function that... I don’t know what a function is.”
“Enable, or at least push, the user to create a successful function on first try”
Not on the first try. On the visit they are ready: “We believe that new users will not be prepared to create from a blank prompt at first”
end: Every line of the brief was answered, one level down from where it was asked.
close: We answer the brief by finding the problem underneath it.
imgs: The scope of work, page by page

q: How do you serve the person who knows what they want, and the one who doesn't?
form: An argument between two people that ends in a rule
subject: One thread of sticky notes between Divya and Kahran
rows: “whats the intent difference with this vs the landing page text?”
“is this intent and curiosity? how are we grabbing intent”
“what if we had search that replaced my library or something? i donno”
“if i>c then things might be more clear?”
end: It became the third bet, in one line: “Favor people who have a goal to complete, and secondarily support people who are curious or idly browsing”
close: We choose who comes first, and then hold to it on every page.
imgs: The round where it was argued

q: How do you decide what not to build?
form: Three no's, each for a different reason
subject: The things turned down, and on whose behalf
rows: The user. It is a worse act than making.
“there is no point in replacing create with a far lower quality action”
“it would be not useful to the buisness.”
“at the moment we dont need to design for that”
end: Three panels. A no is only useful with a reason someone can argue with.
close: We keep the product about one act, and say no to the rest out loud.

q: How do you say what you are in a few words?
form: One slot, one line at a time
subject: The headline, and every line that sat in its place
rows: “these arent AI tools though. They are tools made with AI.”
Each a little off. Each gone.
end: Only the words move. The front page appears around the last one.
close: We write the headline as a design problem, until the product fits inside it.
imgs: The one on the front page

q: How do you get someone to give up a habit that works?
form: Two columns, the same job twice
subject: The pitch against what people already do
rows: It works. You close the tab.
It works. It stays in your library.
It is where you left it
end: The left column never changes. That is the point: “a new way of completing an existing behavior to users, not a new behavior”
close: We design against what people already do, not against an empty space.
imgs: The tools people already use, from the first bet

q: How do you get a team to see its product as a stranger does?
subject: One workshop: the team writing a newcomer's thoughts onto their own product
rows: Their product, drawn as one line
Home, a prompt, a build, a run.
What is a newcomer thinking going into each step, and coming out of it?
“I don’t really know what types of thing I can build with CodeWords”
“what are integrations?” “Do I just sit and wait?” “What is this page for?”
The diagram can hardly be seen under them.
end: Nobody from outside told them what was wrong. It is on the wall, in their words.
close: We get the team to find the problem themselves, so the fix is theirs too.
imgs: The old flow under the team's notes
